/society/2026/nov/22/nhs-savings-hospita.headline: Doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby was barred from treating patients during trial
/society/2026/nov/22/nhs-savings-hospita.excerpt: A senior doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby and who was held up by prosecutors as a pre-eminent expert was barred from treating patients during the trial over fears he posed a risk to their safety. Prof Peter Hindmarsh, a specialist in hormones in children, was crucial to the crown’s argument that the British nurse had poisoned children by injecting insulin into fluid bags. But a Guardian investigation can reveal he was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023, five months before the end of the trial, by his employer, University College London hospitals trust (UCLH). Jurors were never told. Among the reasons for UCLH’s decision was that his advice to child patients relating to insulin was not considered safe. A UCLH medical director told the General Medical Council (GMC), the doctors’ regulator, that the hospital could not “accept the level of risk Professor Hindmarsh appears to pose to children and young people”. The GMC, which was already investigating Hindmarsh’s fitness to practise, subsequently applied for his registration as a doctor to be suspended. That could have resulted in his evidence in the trial of Letby – which was still in progress – being dismissed. However, in April 2023 a medical practitioners tribunal – an independent panel that decides GMC proceedings against doctors – opted not to suspend his registration. Instead, it ordered that Hindmarsh be directly supervised in his work, to protect patient safety.
/society/2026/nov/22/nhs-savings-hospita.trail: Exclusive: Jury was never told that Prof Peter Hindmarsh was barred from practising over concerns for patients’ safety

/society/2026/nov/22/nhs-savings-hospita.headline: UK blood services issue urgent appeal for donations as winter approaches
/society/2026/nov/22/nhs-savings-hospita.excerpt: UK blood services have issued an urgent appeal for 150,000 donations to help the NHS cope with the increase in demand that occurs during the winter. Supplies of blood have run particularly low, with reserves of certain blood types only half of what is considered necessary, officials say. They include supplies of O negative, B negative, O positive and RO blood. People of black heritage have also been asked to donate to help the NHS treat people with sickle cell disease. The health service needs 5,000 donors every day – who either give blood already or are new volunteers – from now until the new year in order to ensure hospitals have enough for patients. That is because blood has a shelf life of 35 days and platelets of just seven days. Blood service officials want people to fill 150,000 donation appointments over the coming weeks and help boost what they stress are “life-saving supplies” of vital products. Each donation takes an hour and can help save three lives, they say. Winter’s cold weather brings two challenges for blood supply agencies. The greater prevalence of colds, coughs and respiratory illnesses such as flu stops people who are unwell from donating. It can also leave people with long-term conditions, including sickle cell disease and cancer, needing to receive more blood or transfusions of platelets to safeguard their health.
/society/2026/nov/22/nhs-savings-hospita.trail: Supplies are low and reserves of certain types are half of what the UK needs, officials say

/society/2026/nov/22/nhs-savings-hospita.headline: How Microsoft outage has affected key public services in the UK
/society/2026/nov/22/nhs-savings-hospita.excerpt: Hospitals, GPs, police forces and property agents across the UK have been hit by the global Microsoft outage. Here’s how the disruption to email and other IT facilities has affected key services. Healthcare The NHS experienced “serious” and “widespread” disruption across the UK on Friday as a result of the Microsoft outage, with hundreds of hospitals, GP surgeries and community health services affected, senior health sources said. While some doctors, hospital workers and NHS night staff told the Guardian they first noticed problems accessing emails during the early hours of Friday morning, the severity of the problem became apparent to most from about 6am. The NHS.net Connect system – which more than 1 million NHS staff use for emails, meetings, calendars, file access and other tasks – is powered by Microsoft. The outage meant many could not log in, perform basic duties, or send and receive patient data needed for the delivery of healthcare. NHS sources said the outage caused disruption to a range of Microsoft 365 services relied upon by staff, including Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive and Copilot. The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) also said it was experiencing problems sending and receiving emails. Some staff resorted to using patients’ paper records after being unable to access email and other IT facilities.
/society/2026/nov/22/nhs-savings-hospita.trail: Hospitals, GPs, police forces and property agents have had to find a workaround for Microsoft packages

/society/2026/nov/22/nhs-savings-hospita.headline: Microsoft outage hits hospitals, GPs, schools and police across UK
/society/2026/nov/22/nhs-savings-hospita.excerpt: Vital UK services have been hit by a global Microsoft outage that left hospital staff resorting to paper records and fuelled concerns about an over-reliance on a small number of tech companies. A day of widespread disruption sent some sectors back to the 1990s, with court staff looking for fax machines and rail travellers being warned they might not be able to rely on digital tickets. Schools, universities and businesses were also hit by the global outage affecting Microsoft’s 365 suite of products, which began late on Thursday evening and interrupted access to emails and calendars. Hundreds of hospitals, GP surgeries and community health services were affected as the NHS struggled to confirm appointment times, pharmacists warned of delays to prescriptions and a union reported that ambulance services had suffered a “serious impact”. The NHS.net Connect system – which more than one million NHS staff use for emails, meetings, calendars, file access and other tasks – is powered by Microsoft. The outage meant many could not log in, perform basic duties, or send and receive patient data needed for the delivery of healthcare. Police forces told people to contact them by telephone if they needed to report crimes, instead of using online forms.
/society/2026/nov/22/nhs-savings-hospita.trail: NHS suffering ‘serious’ and widespread disruption, while people are told of possible delays in receiving prescriptions

/society/2026/nov/22/nhs-savings-hospita.headline: Rise in NHS birth centre closures ‘shocking’ denial of women’s rights, experts say
/society/2026/nov/22/nhs-savings-hospita.excerpt: NHS officials are shutting growing numbers of birth centres in a “shocking” denial of a woman’s right to have a midwife rather than a doctor oversee their baby’s birth, say campaigners. Twelve birth centres – midwife-led maternity units – have closed in England since 2019. Birth centres play a key role in ensuring that women can choose whether to have their baby at a unit in a hospital run by doctors, at one where midwives are in charge, or at home. Six units have shut permanently since Labour came to power in July 2024. Four others have been closed “temporarily” for so long, up to six years, that childbirth groups fear they will never reopen. Two other birth centres closed because the hospitals where they were based have begun to fall apart and will remain out of action for several years until new facilities are built. Women’s ability to choose where their baby is born is also being increasingly restricted in England and Wales by NHS bodies suspending home birth services for up to 14 months. The wave of closures and suspensions is occurring because of the NHS-wide shortage of midwives, a falling birthrate, the growing complexity of childbirth and a rise in caesarean sections. Campaigners say the loss of local childbirth services is denying women their right to choose and forcing them to travel from their home area to give birth.
/society/2026/nov/22/nhs-savings-hospita.trail: Twelve midwife-led maternity units have closed in England since 2019 with six closing since Labour came to power in 2024

/environment/2026/nov/22/cop31-climate-t.headline: ‘Difficult geopolitical times’: Albanese defends Bowen after Cop31 deal failure
/environment/2026/nov/22/cop31-climate-t.excerpt: Anthony Albanese has defended Chris Bowen from criticism following the failure of the UN Cop31 climate summit, blaming the result on “difficult geopolitical times” as the Coalition called for the minister to resign. Bowen served as president of negotiations at the talks in Turkey, helping run the conference with his Turkish counterpart, Murat Kurum. Speaking to journalists late on Sunday after a list of countries rejected a proposed “cover decision” – an overarching agreement – for the conference, Bowen said “Australia left nothing on the field” but the “red lines” he and his staff tried to negotiate to find consensus between nearly 200 countries were unbridgeable. The biggest sticking point was whether the agreement would mention the need for the world to transition away from fossil fuels. The European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, Norway and Belize told the conference they would not accept a deal without it. Saudi Arabia and Russia led a group of oil-rich countries that vowed to veto a decision that included mention of fossil fuels. Bowen told reporters: “I would have been happy with [a] transition away from fossil fuels being in the text, but that was not going to get support.” He said despite the breakdown, “in the real world” the transition away from fossil fuels was inevitable and happening at speed.
/environment/2026/nov/22/cop31-climate-t.trail: Coalition calls for climate change minister to resign immediately or be sacked over ‘catastrophic diplomatic disaster’, despite offering no alternatives on reducing emissions

/environment/2026/nov/22/cop31-climate-t.headline: Cop31 left Chris Bowen stuck between petrostates and climate reality. But the f-word failure is not his alone
/environment/2026/nov/22/cop31-climate-t.excerpt: After delivering a major speech to the UN climate talks in Turkey last week, the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, dismissed criticisms that he hadn’t managed to name the problem that is overwhelmingly driving catastrophic global heating – burning fossil fuels. “You could pick out any number of things that were not in what was a short speech,” he later said. If Albanese really thought the head of a leading coal and gas exporter failing to address the issue head-on was inconsequential or trivial, then his climate change minister, Chris Bowen, will have a story for him after the finals days of the fractious talks that became the longest UN climate summit ever. Those talks failed spectacularly to nail its prime ambition – an “Antalya pact” that was meant to drive investment in renewable energy and electrification, boost finance to help developing countries facing worsening climate damage, and acknowledge the world is bursting through a goal of limiting the increase in global temperatures to 1.5C, with alarming consequences across the planet. As president of negotiations, Bowen barely slept for three days, and on the final night caught only a few moments of shut-eye on a couch in the office where a parade of negotiators had been coming to sit and talk to him.
/environment/2026/nov/22/cop31-climate-t.trail: Australia’s climate change minister will face a torrent of criticism over his role, but disagreement over fossil fuels proved an unbridgeable sticking point

/environment/2026/nov/22/cop31-climate-t.headline: Finance, fossil fuels and the ‘overshoot’: six key takeaways from Cop31
/environment/2026/nov/22/cop31-climate-t.excerpt: As the planet faces the devastating impacts of unprecedented human-caused global heating, close to 200 countries have been meeting in Antalya, Turkey, for the annual UN climate summit. Here are six key takeaways from Cop31. Fossil fuels cannot be ignored These talks fell apart over the refusal by some countries to allow mention of fossil fuels in the final “cover decision” text – the “Antalya pact” – and the refusal of others to agree an outcome without it. Yet for most people watching, it will seem absurd for a climate conference not to address the actual cause of global heating. The EU, the UK, a handful of other rich nations and scores of developing countries, including the most vulnerable small islands and the least developed countries, joined in a loose coalition of about 130 parties on Saturday night to demand recognition of the need to “transition away from fossil fuels” in the final outcome of Cop31. Their demands failed but the issue will not go away. All countries agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels” at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023. That original promise still stands and has not been repudiated, but refusing to talk about fossil fuels seems no longer a tenable position for the only global climate forum. Finance matters Although developing nations made up most of the 130 countries banded together in a “progressive coalition”, many of those countries did not object in the final session of Cop31 to the “Antalya pact”.
/environment/2026/nov/22/cop31-climate-t.trail: Fractious summit has highlighted need for wider consensus and more astute handling of the negotiations

/environment/2026/nov/22/cop31-climate-t.headline: Climate talks stall as countries mull showdown with Saudi Arabia over fossil fuel phaseout
/environment/2026/nov/22/cop31-climate-t.excerpt: Climate talks reached a standstill on Saturday night in Turkey as some countries mulled whether to force a showdown with Saudi Arabia and its allies over the global need to phase out fossil fuels. The co-conveners of the Cop31 UN climate summit, Australia’s Chris Bowen and Turkey’s Murat Kurum, held meetings with scores of countries throughout Saturday until late evening as the fortnight-long talks overran without resolution, with countries and campaigners growing increasingly frustrated at the lack of progress. The key sticking points concerned the insistence by a loose coalition of about 130 countries on including a reference to the “transition away from fossil fuels” in the final outcome of the talks, as well as demands by developing countries to bolster their rights to funding from the rich world to help them adapt to the escalating impacts of the climate crisis. Saudi Arabia and some other oil-rich nations have consistently opposed an explicit statement on fossil fuel use. A third draft of a potential headline agreement, released in the early hours on Sunday, attempted to address the impasse by saying countries recalled a deal reached in Dubai three years ago – the only summit at which countries have reached consensus on the need to move away from burning coal, oil and gas. Maina Talia, climate minister for the low-lying Pacific island Tuvalu, said: “This [inclusion of a reference to fossil fuels] is a red line for us. We’re talking about the root cause of all this.
/environment/2026/nov/22/cop31-climate-t.trail: New draft text released at Cop31 summit after countries fail to agree on electrification and finance for developing world

/environment/2026/nov/22/cop31-climate-t.headline: What’s left to do as Cop31 enters its frantic final days
/environment/2026/nov/22/cop31-climate-t.excerpt: The end is in sight. If all goes as planned, countries as diverse as wealthy petrostates erecting new oil rigs and low-lying islands threatened by rising seas will reach an agreement tomorrow in Antalya, bringing the 31st UN climate summit to a close (though, as usual, the talks are likely to overrun). But tensions – much like our global temperatures – are running high. A draft text that satisfies all the competing interests is a long way off, and negotiators are expected to argue into the night and then the weekend. On the table are the electrification of the global economy, the transition away from fossil fuels, and the response to the looming overshoot of the 1.5C (2.7F) temperature target. Deepening the divide are long-running disputes over who should pay what, and emerging fights over the fairness of the transition and assumptions in the underlying science. I’ve been following the contentious climate talks from afar every day for our liveblog, as my tireless colleagues on the ground have raced from interview to interview. The three big issues frustrating diplomats help the rest of us make sense of how well humanity is doing at keeping the planet habitable. Here’s what stands out, and what’s at stake in these final days. But first, the headlines.
/environment/2026/nov/22/cop31-climate-t.trail: The diplomatic battles shaping the future of climate action as Cop31 enters its final days

/world/2026/nov/23/israel-gaza-destructi.headline: Israeli tanks cross ‘yellow line’ boundary into Hamas-controlled central Gaza
/world/2026/nov/23/israel-gaza-destructi.excerpt: The Israeli military crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza on Wednesday in its first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed last October, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents. Israeli tanks rolled along the Salah al-Din road, Gaza’s main north-south route, a day after the US-backed Board of Peace, a body overseeing the ceasefire, accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities. An Israeli military spokesperson said troops were carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of the yellow line in central Gaza. The operation lasted about 24 hours and on Thursday the military said it had been “completed”. The IDF has not commented extensively on the operation, which came as the Israeli opposition politician, Gadi Eisenkot, has been seeking to form a government without the caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has built his political reputation on promises to keep Israel safe. A Gaza security source told AFP there was “intense Israeli artillery shelling” north of Nuseirat refugee camp and reported Israeli military vehicles in central Gaza “amid ongoing gunfire and airstrikes since midday”. Hamas condemned the Israeli raid and the forced displacement of Palestinians as “a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement” and a dangerous escalation. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Hamas’s statement.
/world/2026/nov/23/israel-gaza-destructi.trail: First incursion across boundary since ceasefire deal comes as Eisenkot seeks to form government without Netanyahu

/world/2026/nov/23/israel-gaza-destructi.headline: ‘They want silence’: how the film NAZA is shaking Israel
/world/2026/nov/23/israel-gaza-destructi.excerpt: It was on Yom Kippur this year that Nadav Weiman first sensed the documentary NAZA was having a significant impact in Israel – despite the fact that back in September, when the Jewish festival fell, barely a handful of Israelis had seen the film. NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and will stream for free on its website in early December, depicts 24 army intelligence officers interviewed anonymously on rooftops across Tel Aviv. They talk about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza over the past three years, and the secret signoff system employed by Israel’s military. More than 1.5 million people have already seen it in cinemas and its Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor have picked up a roster of prestigious awards. The film has been offered to a number of distributors and cinemas in Israel but has not been screened there yet, amid a severe backlash. Weiman lives in Shapira, a secular, left-leaning suburb of Tel Aviv. Days before the high holy day, NAZA had premiered at the Venice film festival to a 25-minute standing ovation. As Weiman mooched between friends and neighbours on the public holiday, almost everyone was discussing the documentary. The tenor of reaction was almost universally hostile, he concedes, even among his more liberal peers. “Yes, almost all had very hardline views about the movie” he tells me.
/world/2026/nov/23/israel-gaza-destructi.trail: The documentary has triggered fierce backlash, but by exposing the army’s conduct in Gaza it’s proved impossible to ignore

/world/2026/nov/23/israel-gaza-destructi.headline: Children at risk as ‘weaponisation of aid’ surges in conflict zones, analysis finds
/world/2026/nov/23/israel-gaza-destructi.excerpt: The “weaponisation” of aid is becoming normalised, with new analysis revealing that deliberate holding back of humanitarian help to children in conflict zones has increased 16-fold in the past decade. The assessment of UN-verified incidents corroborates concerns that denying vital aid is becoming a common tactic of modern warfare. Cases where children were denied access to humanitarian aid was proven to have increased from 509 in 2015 to 8,322 last year, according to an analysis by Save the Children. On Sunday the UK, Australia, Canada and Italy urged Israel to allow critical aid into Gaza to help displaced people trapped in flimsy shelters as the first heavy rains of the winter hit. An infant drowned and three children and a mother were killed last week when storms lashed the besieged territory, as Israel refuse to allow 150,000 tents and other vital supplies past its border controls. The data analysis estimates that more than a fifth of all violations against children in conflict recorded by the UN now involve the denial of aid – up from 2% a decade ago. Orlaith Minogue, head of humanitarian advocacy at Save the Children UK, said: “We are witnessing an unprecedented surge in the weaponisation of aid alongside a wider collapse in international cooperation and escalating climate crises. “Children are uniquely vulnerable in conflict and climate disasters.
/world/2026/nov/23/israel-gaza-destructi.trail: New assessment shows large increase in cases where access to humanitarian help is deliberately restricted, with most incidents in Palestine

/world/2026/nov/23/israel-gaza-destructi.headline: Revealed: Israel uploaded millions of photos to Amazon’s facial recognition platform to track Palestinians
/world/2026/nov/23/israel-gaza-destructi.excerpt: The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians, the Guardian can reveal. Leaked documents show the expansive catalogue of images was moved into Amazon’s cloud in the early months of Israel’s devastating aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza. The images were uploaded by a department of the Israeli military that holds a vast collection of photos covering the Palestinian populations in Gaza and the West Bank. The department informed Amazon of the decision to upload the images in early 2024 so it could use Rekognition, the company’s AI-powered image analysis platform for a facial recognition project. The documents obtained by the Guardian form part of an investigation into the Israeli military’s reliance on the technology and infrastructure of Amazon’s cloud computing business to monitor Palestinians. According to the files and interviews with military sources, Israel has in recent years migrated huge volumes of data – including sensitive intelligence material and information about Palestinians living under occupation – into Amazon’s datacentres. The large set of images was moved into an Amazon datacentre near Tel Aviv by a department commonly known as Rolling Stone, which sits within a military software unit.
/world/2026/nov/23/israel-gaza-destructi.trail: Upload came as the Israeli military was increasing its reliance on Amazon’s cloud platform to meet the technological demands of its bombardment of Gaza

/world/2026/nov/23/israel-gaza-destructi.headline: NAZA: how and where to watch the Guardian’s acclaimed Gaza documentary
/world/2026/nov/23/israel-gaza-destructi.excerpt: Where can I watch the film? NAZA will be released in full on the Guardian’s website for free in early December. Sign up here to be notified of the exact streaming date and to be sent a link to the film when it is live. NAZA is currently screening in cinemas all over the world. It has been shown by cinemas in 47 countries and seen by more than 1.5 million people since its release last month, making it one of the most-watched documentary films with a theatrical release in 2026. The film has been offered to a number of distributors and cinemas in Israel but has not been screened there yet. You can watch a trailer here. What is NAZA about? NAZA is a documentary featuring testimony from 24 Israeli military intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians during the war in Gaza. The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to civilians expected to be killed in a military attack. The interviewees detail the methods used by the Israeli military in Gaza, including AI-based systems built to identify large numbers of potential Hamas operatives, who were then bombed in their homes at night, in the knowledge that the attacks would also kill their families. Interviews were filmed at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv, on the condition of anonymity, because of the risks involved in speaking publicly.
/world/2026/nov/23/israel-gaza-destructi.trail: Film features testimony from 24 Israeli officials involved in surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians

/society/2026/nov/22/pip-review-overhaul.headline: Alan Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people
/society/2026/nov/22/pip-review-overhaul.excerpt: Andy Burnham is being urged to spend billions of pounds on a “new deal” for the next generation that would fund guaranteed jobs support for young people to offset a radical cut in benefits. In a watershed report on Britain’s youth jobs crisis, Alan Milburn, the Tony Blair-era health secretary, said the country was at a “fork in the road” after a surge in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost a million. He said ministers had a choice to either carry on down a path of state and market failure or adopt a 10-year plan with an ambition to eradicate long-term youth unemployment. Publishing a blueprint for change in a highly anticipated review, the report calls on the government to launch a sweeping shake-up of welfare, education, health and employment policy with the aim to ensure every young person has the chance to earn or learn. If adopted by the government, Britain could halve the number of young people neither earning nor learning, helping about 600,000 more under-25s into education, employment or training each year by 2036, according to the review. Milburn’s report comes as Britain’s young bear the brunt of rising joblessness as employers freeze their hiring plans amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East. Coupled with the legacies of the Covid pandemic and austerity, and a rise in mental ill-health and as AI upends the jobs market, the UK’s Neet rate has reached 13% – the highest level since 2014.
/society/2026/nov/22/pip-review-overhaul.trail: Report on Britain’s youth jobs crisis calls for welfare, education, health and employment policy shake-up

/society/2026/nov/22/pip-review-overhaul.headline: No 10 considering expanding under-25s benefits overhaul to older age groups
/society/2026/nov/22/pip-review-overhaul.excerpt: Downing Street is considering whether plans to replace key disability benefits with work and training for people under-25 should be expanded to older age groups, the Guardian has learned, in a move that risks reigniting Labour tensions over welfare changes. Andy Burnham and other cabinet ministers are looking at applying the idea of “participation first” to all people of working age, meaning spending billions more on support to enter the workplace while cutting or removing some disability benefits. The move would be politically risky given the difficulties that Keir Starmer faced in getting changes to health and disability benefits past the Labour parliamentary party last year, with a rebellion leading to a major U-turn. The government is preparing to accept recommendations from its adviser, Alan Milburn, next week on overhauling the benefits system for young people. In his report, Milburn will propose that under-25s should get training and support instead of the universal credit health element. Under the plans, young people with disabilities will also lose their personal independence payment (Pip) but will be able to apply to a local fund for specific short-term expenses and equipment, rather than an ongoing payment. Those with the most extreme needs who cannot work will have their entitlements protected.
/society/2026/nov/22/pip-review-overhaul.trail: Exclusive: Plans to replace key disability benefits for young people with work and training could affect adults

/society/2026/nov/22/pip-review-overhaul.headline: Healey vows to cut welfare bill before next election with ‘tough’ approach to young people
/society/2026/nov/22/pip-review-overhaul.excerpt: John Healey had said there will be a reduction in the welfare bill before the next election, with a “tough” approach to young people who do not accept support to get a job or training. The chancellor was repeatedly pressed on the issue in broadcast interviews after documents from the Office for Budget Responsibility suggested sickness and disability benefits would cost £100bn a year before the end of the decade. Healey delivered a budget on Wednesday with small giveaways for most households such as £100 off energy bills to help ease the cost of living. But he deferred some difficult decisions on how defence spending at 3% of national income would be paid for and did not set out any changes to welfare – both of which are likely to be addressed at the spending review. Speaking after the budget, Healey told BBC Radio 4’s Today: “We have to bring the benefits bill down.” He echoed the words of Andy Burnham when he said there would be no “crude cuts” after Keir Starmer’s attempts to cut disability benefits were stopped by Labour MPs. But he said the welfare system was “unsustainable” and that the government would set out changes after two big reports on how it could be overhauled: the Milburn review of young people and work and the Timms review of the disability benefit system.
/society/2026/nov/22/pip-review-overhaul.trail: Chancellor’s comments come as fiscal watchdog says disability benefits will cost £100bn a year before end of decade

/news/2026/nov/22/russell-brand-wife-lau.headline: Prison authorities consider whether Russell Brand harassed victims with YouTube message
/news/2026/nov/22/russell-brand-wife-lau.excerpt: The prison authorities are weighing up whether Russell Brand harassed his victims by issuing comments through his wife insisting he was not guilty of rape and sexual assault. After Andy Burnham called on Google to take down the statement from YouTube, a continuing Ministry of Justice inquiry is focusing on whether Brand has broken rules that are supposed to prevent “serious distress” to the victims of crime. Other factors that will help to decide whether he has broken a rule include the “notoriety” of the crimes and the length of time between the verdict and the statement. A video in which Brand’s wife, Laura Gallacher, read out a message from the jailed sex offender protesting he was not guilty has remained on YouTube days after ministers asked for it to be removed. Brand is serving a 10-and-a-half-year term after he was convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November. On Thursday night, the UK prime minister said he “wouldn’t leap” to changing the law to force social media companies to take down the content. But he added: “I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down. “You know, why are we having to hear from from him?
/news/2026/nov/22/russell-brand-wife-lau.trail: Ministry of Justice weighs up comments issued through rapist’s wife as PM asks: ‘Why are we having to hear from him?’

/news/2026/nov/22/russell-brand-wife-lau.headline: Ministry of Justice investigating Russell Brand message from prison claiming he is not guilty
/news/2026/nov/22/russell-brand-wife-lau.excerpt: The Ministry of Justice has launched an investigation into whether Russell Brand has broken prison rules after the jailed comedian shared a message claiming he was not guilty of sexual offences just days after his conviction. Brand’s wife, Laura Brand, read a message from her husband, who was convicted of rape, in a video uploaded to their YouTube channel in which he claimed: “I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for.” If found to have broken the rules, Brand could face sanctions ranging from an extension of his sentence to loss of privileges such as access to a telephone for a limited period. It is understood a prisoner will be deemed to have broken the rules if they provide comments to a family member that they know will be published. Asked about the comments, the prime minister’s official spokesperson said: “This is clearly appalling and is being urgently investigated. We expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules. “Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances. Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments … This is being urgently investigated. We expect action to be taken if the rules have been broken.” Brand, 51, is serving a 10-and-a-half-year prison term after he was convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November.
/news/2026/nov/22/russell-brand-wife-lau.trail: PM’s spokesperson calls message, read out by convicted rapist’s wife on their YouTube channel, ‘clearly appalling’
